In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿God has indeed heard﴾. Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisaʾi read it with idgham (assimilation) of the dal into the sin, while the rest read it with izhar (clear pronunciation) of the dal.

Al-Kisaʾi said: "Whoever makes the dal clear before the sin, his tongue is non-Arabic (ʿajami) and not Arabic." ﴿The statement of her who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾, meaning she argues with you about the matter of her husband, ﴿and complains to God﴾, is coordinated (ʿaṭf) on "disputes with you."

The dispute in question was this: whenever he said to her, "You have become unlawful to me," she would say, "By God, he has not mentioned divorce." Then she would say, "I complain to God of my poverty and my loneliness, and I have young children: if I join them to him, they are lost, and if I join them to me, they go hungry." She began raising her head to the sky and saying, "O God, I complain to You." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and complains to God﴾.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: This verse was revealed about Khawla bint Thaʿlaba and her husband Aws ibn al-Samit, who had a touch of madness (lamam). One day his madness intensified, and he performed ẓihār against her (zihar, a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a man likens his wife to a woman forbidden to him, such as his mother), then he regretted it. At that time, ẓihār was a form of divorce in the Jahiliyya.

It was also said that she was Khawla bint Hakim, and it was said that her name was Jamila. The first view is more sound. It was also said that she was the daughter of Khuwaylid.

Al-Mawardi said: She was attributed sometimes to her father and sometimes to her grandfather, and both are correct: her father and her grandfather. So she is Khawla bint Thaʿlaba ibn Khuwaylid.

The clause ﴿God hears your conversation﴾ is either in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or it is a resumed clause (mustaʾnafa) functioning as a reason (taʿlil) for what precedes it. That is: God knows your mutual argument in speech.

﴿Indeed God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾: He hears everything that is heard and sees everything that is seen, and among that is what this woman argued with you about.

Then He, glorified be He, explained the matter of ẓihār itself and mentioned its ruling, saying: ﴿Those of you who perform ẓihār against their wives﴾. The majority read yuẓahharūn (يَظَّهَّرُونَ) with shadda and a fatḥa on the first letter of the imperfect. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi read yuẓāhirūn (يُظّاهِرُونَ) with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, shadda on the ẓāʾ, and an added alif. Abu al-ʿAliya, ʿAsim, and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh read yuẓāhirūn (يُظاهِرُونَ) with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, a light pronunciation of the ẓāʾ, and a kasra on the hāʾ.

Something similar to this has already been discussed in Surat al-Aḥzab.

The meaning of ẓihār is that a man says to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother." There is no disagreement that this is ẓihār.

They differed if he says, "You are to me like the back of my daughter," or "my sister," or anything else of those women who are unlawful to him by kinship. A group, including Abu Ḥanifa and Malik, held that this is ẓihār, and this was the view of al-Ḥasan, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Zuhri, al-Awzaʿi, and al-Thawri.

A group including Qatada and al-Shaʿbi said that it is not ẓihār, but that ẓihār is specific to the mother alone.

The narrations from al-Shafiʿi differed: it was narrated from him in the manner of the first view, and it was narrated from him in the manner of the second view. The root of ẓihār is derived from ẓahr (back).

They differed if he says to his wife, "You are to me like the head of my mother, or her hand, or her leg, or something similar." Is it ẓihār or not? The same applies if he says, "You are to me like my mother," without mentioning the back. The apparent view is that if he intends ẓihār by that, it is ẓihār.

It was narrated from Abu Ḥanifa that if he likens her to a part of his mother's body which it is permissible for him to look at, it is not ẓihār.

It was narrated from al-Shafiʿi that ẓihār occurs only when it is by the back alone.

They differed if he likens his wife to a foreign woman. It was said that it is ẓihār, and it was said that it is not. The discussion of this is extensive in the books of furūʿ (positive law).

The clause ﴿they are not their mothers﴾ is in the nominative position (maḥall rafʿ), as the predicate of the relative clause. That is: their wives are not their mothers. So that is a lie on their part, and in this there is rebuke and reproach for those who perform ẓihār.

The majority read ʾummahātihim (أُمَّهاتِهِمْ) in the accusative, according to the Ḥijazi dialect in which mā functions like laysa (in governing the predicate). Abu ʿAmr and al-Sulami read it in the nominative, without this governing, and this is the dialect of Najd and Banu Asad.

Then He, glorified be He, explained to them who their mothers truly are, saying: ﴿Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them﴾. That is: their mothers are only the women who bore them.

Then He increased in rebuke and censure of them, saying: ﴿And indeed they utter an objectionable word and a lie﴾. That is: those who perform ẓihār indeed utter with this statement an objectionable word, that is, a repugnant word that the Sharīʿa rejects. Zūr (زُورًا) means falsehood. Munkaran and zūran are in the accusative because they are adjectives of a verbal noun that has been omitted, meaning: a statement that is objectionable and false.

﴿And indeed God is Most Pardoning, Most Forgiving﴾: that is, abundant in pardon and forgiveness, since He made the expiation (kaffāra) upon them a means of freeing them from this objectionable statement.

﴿And those who perform ẓihār against their wives, then go back on what they said﴾. When He, glorified be He, mentioned ẓihār in general and rebuked those who commit it, He began detailing its rulings. The meaning is: those who say that objectionable and false statement, then go back on what they said, that is, return to what they said by making amends and retracting it, as in His saying: ﴿that you should never return to the like of it﴾ (Qur'an 24:17), that is, to its like.

Al-Akhfash said: "li-mā qālū" (لِما قالُوا) and "ilā mā qālū" (إلى ما قالُوا) are interchangeable. He cited: ﴿And they said, "Praise belongs to God, who guided us to this"﴾ (7:43); and He said: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ (37:23); and He said: ﴿because your Lord has inspired her﴾ (99:5); and He said: ﴿And it was revealed to Noah﴾ (11:36).

Al-Farrāʾ said: the lām (ل) has the sense of "ʿan" (عَنْ, "from"), and the meaning is: then they retract what they said and intend intercourse.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: then they return to the intention of sexual intercourse on account of what they said.

Al-Akhfash also said: the verse has inversion (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr). The meaning is: those who perform ẓihār against their wives, then go back to what they were doing of intercourse, ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾ for what they said, that is: upon them is the freeing of a neck on account of what they said.

So the preposition in His saying "li-mā qālū" is connected to the omitted element which is the predicate of the subject, which is "upon them" (fa-ʿalayhim).

The people of knowledge differed in interpreting the mentioned "return" (ʿawd) in several views:

The first: it is the determination to have intercourse. This was said by the Iraqis, Abu Ḥanifa and his companions. It was also narrated from Malik.

It was said: it is the intercourse itself. This was said by al-Ḥasan, and it was also narrated from Malik.

It was said: it is that he keeps her as a wife after ẓihār while having the ability to divorce. This was said by al-Shafiʿi.

It was said: it is the expiation, and the meaning is that he may not have intercourse with her except by means of expiation. This was said by al-Layth ibn Saʿd, and it was narrated from Abu Ḥanifa.

It was said: it is repeating the ẓihār by its wording. This was said by the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Ẓāhir). It was narrated from Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj, Abu al-ʿAliya, and al-Farrāʾ. The meaning is: then they return to the statement of what they said.

The relative clause is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾, on the assumption of "upon them the freeing of a neck," as mentioned earlier. Or: then what is obligatory upon them is the manumission of a neck. One says ḥarrartuhu (حَرَّرْتُهُ), meaning: I made him free. The apparent view is that any neck suffices. It was said that it must be a believing neck, like the neck in the expiation for murder. The first view was held by Abu Ḥanifa and his companions, and the second by Malik and al-Shafiʿi, who also required that it be free of every defect.

﴿Before they touch one another﴾: the touching here means intercourse. This was said by the majority. So it is not permissible for the one who performed ẓihār to have intercourse until he makes expiation. It was said that the intended meaning is enjoyment through intercourse, touching, or looking at the private part with desire. This was said by Malik, and it is one of the two views of al-Shafiʿi.

The indication in His saying: ﴿That﴾ refers to the ruling mentioned, and it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿you are admonished with it﴾, that is, you are commanded with it, or you are restrained from committing ẓihār by it. In this is a clarification of what the purpose of prescribing expiation is.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: "That [is] the severity of the expiation by which you are admonished": that is, the severity of the expiation is an admonition to you so that you abandon ẓihār.

﴿And God is Acquainted with what you do﴾: nothing of your deeds is hidden from Him, so He will reward you for them.

Then He, glorified be He, mentioned the ruling for one who is unable to perform the expiation, saying: ﴿So whoever does not find [a neck], then fasting two consecutive months before they touch one another﴾. That is: whoever does not find a neck in his possession and is not able to obtain its value, then upon him is fasting two consecutive months, successive, without breaking the fast during them. If he breaks it, he begins again if the breaking was without an excuse. If it was due to an excuse such as travel or illness, then Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabāḥ, ʿAmr ibn Dinar, al-Shaʿbi, al-Shafiʿi, and Malik said: he continues and does not begin again.

Abu Ḥanifa said: he begins again. This is also narrated from al-Shafiʿi. The meaning of "before they touch one another" is what was mentioned shortly before. So if he has intercourse by night or day, intentionally or by mistake, he begins again. This was said by Abu Ḥanifa and Malik.

Al-Shafiʿi said: he does not begin again if he has intercourse by night, because the night is not a time for fasting. The first view is more preferable.

﴿So whoever is not able﴾, meaning: to fast two consecutive months, ﴿then feeding sixty needy persons﴾: that is, upon him is to feed sixty needy persons, two mudd (مُدّ) for each needy person, which is half a ṣāʿ. This was said by Abu Ḥanifa and his companions.

Al-Shafiʿi and others said: one mudd for each needy person. The apparent meaning of the verse is that he feeds them until they are satisfied once, or gives them what satisfies them. He is not obligated to gather them all at once; rather he may feed some of the sixty on one day and others on another day.

The indication in His saying: ﴿That﴾ refers to the rulings mentioned earlier, and it is the subject, and its predicate is omitted, meaning: that is in effect, ﴿so that you may believe in God and His Messenger﴾. It is also permissible for the demonstrative to be in the accusative position, and the estimate would be: We have done that so that you may believe, that is, so that you may affirm that God commanded it and legislated it, or so that you may obey God and His Messenger in commands and prohibitions, stop at the limits of the Sharīʿa, not transgress them, and not return to ẓihār, which is an objectionable and false statement.

The indication in His saying: ﴿And these﴾ refers to the rulings mentioned, and it is the subject, and its predicate is "the limits of God." So do not transgress His limits which He set for you, for He has made clear to you that ẓihār is disobedience, and that its expiation mentioned here brings pardon and forgiveness. ﴿And for the disbelievers﴾, those who do not stop at the limits of God and do not act by what God has set for His servants, ﴿there is a painful punishment﴾, which is the punishment of Hell. He called it disbelief (kufr) as an intensification and severity.

Ibn Māja, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "Blessed is He whose hearing encompasses everything! Indeed I heard the speech of Khawla bint Thaʿlaba, and some of it was hidden from me, while she was complaining about her husband to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and she was saying: 'O Messenger of God, my youth has been consumed by him, and I have spread out my belly for him [bearing children]; until when my age has grown old and my children have ceased, he has performed ẓihār against me. O God, I complain to You.'" She said: "She did not leave until Gabriel descended with these verses: ﴿God has indeed heard the statement of her who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾." He was Aws ibn al-Ṣāmit.

Al-Naḥḥas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The first person to perform ẓihār in Islam was Aws. He had a paternal cousin's daughter named Khawla bint Khuwaylid, and he performed ẓihār against her. He was dismayed, and said: 'I see you have become unlawful to me.' So go to the Prophet (ﷺ) and ask him." She came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and found with him the one who combed his hair, and she informed him. He said: "O Khawla, we have not been commanded anything regarding your matter." Then God revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "O Khawla, rejoice." She said: "Good." He said: "Good." Then he recited to her: ﴿God has indeed heard the statement of her who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾ and the verses.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 58, verses 1–4 (part 2 of 2):

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related, by way of Yusuf ibn Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "Khawlah bint Tha'labah narrated to me, saying: 'By Allah, it was concerning me and Aws ibn al-Samit that Allah revealed the opening of Surat al-Mujadilah.' She said: 'I was with him, and he was an elderly man whose temper had become bad. He came in to me one day and I argued with him about something, and he became angry and said: "You are to me like the back of my mother" (anti 'alayya ka-zahri ummi). Then he went out and sat in his people's gathering for a while, then came in to me, and behold, he wanted me for himself. I said: "No, by Him in whose hand is Khawlah's soul! You shall not reach me, after what you have said, until Allah and His Messenger judge concerning us."' Then I went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him of that. I had not left before the Qur'an was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was overcome by what usually overcame him, then it was lifted from him, and he said to me: 'O Khawlah, Allah has revealed concerning you and your companion.' Then he recited to me: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of she who argues with you﴾ until His words: ﴿a painful punishment﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Tell him to free a slave.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he has no means to free a slave.' He said: 'Then let him fast two consecutive months.' I said: 'By Allah, he is an elderly man who has no capacity for fasting.' He said: 'Then let him feed sixty needy persons, a wasq of dates.' I said: 'By Allah, he does not have that.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I will assist him with an 'araq of dates.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I too will assist him with another 'araq.' He said: 'You have done right and done well. Go and give it in charity on his behalf, then treat your cousin kindly.' She said: 'So I did.'" There are other hadiths on this topic.

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi, in his Sunan, related from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿then they return to what they said﴾, that he said: "It is the man who says to his wife: 'You are to me like the back of my mother.' When he says this, it is not lawful for him to approach her, by marriage or otherwise, until he atones by freeing a slave. If he does not find one, then [he must fast] two consecutive months before they touch one another. 'Touching' means intercourse. If he is unable, then [he must feed] sixty needy persons. If he says to her, 'You are to me like the back of my mother if you do such-and-such,' then zihar (the pre-Islamic divorce formula of likening a wife to one's mother) does not take effect in that until he breaks the condition; if he breaks it, he must not approach her until he atones. Divorce does not take effect through zihar."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "Three [acts of atonement] are each a mudd: the expiation for an oath, the expiation for zihar, and the expiation for [breaking a] fast."

al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I have made zihar from my wife, and I saw the whiteness of her anklet in the light of the moon, and I had intercourse with her before I had atoned.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Did Allah not say: "before they touch one another"?' He said: 'I have done it, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Refrain from her until you atone.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have made zihar from my wife and I had intercourse with her before I had atoned.' He said: 'What led you to that?' He said: 'I saw her anklet in the light of the moon.' He said: 'Do not approach her until you do what Allah has commanded you.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Ansari, who said: "I was a man who had been given more desire for women than anyone else. When Ramadan came, I made zihar from my wife until Ramadan should end, out of fear that I might have intercourse with her during my nights, and so I would continue in that and not be able to restrain myself until morning overtook me. Then one night, while she was serving me, something of her was uncovered to me, and I pounced upon her. When I rose in the morning, I went out to my people and told them my account. I said: 'Come with me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and inform him of my matter.' They said: 'No, by Allah, we will not do that. We fear that the Qur'an may be revealed concerning us, or that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) may say about us a saying whose shame will remain upon us. But go yourself and do what seems right to you.' So I went out and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him my account. He said: 'Is it so with you?' I said: 'It is so with me.' He said: 'Is it so with you?' I said: 'It is so with me.' He said: 'Is it so with you?' I said: 'It is so with me. Here I am, so execute upon me the judgment of Allah, for I am patient in that.' He said: 'Free a slave.' I struck my neck with my hand and said: 'No, by Him who sent you with the truth, I have not come to own anything but this.' He said: 'Then fast two consecutive months.' I said: 'Has what befell me befallen me except through fasting?' He said: 'Then feed sixty needy persons.' I said: 'By Him who sent you with the truth, we spent this night of ours hungry, with no supper.' He said: 'Go to the official in charge of the charity of Banu Zurayq, and tell him to hand it over to you, and feed sixty needy persons from it with a wasq on your behalf, and then use the rest of it for yourself and your dependants.' So I returned to my people and said: 'I found among you narrowness and bad judgment, and I found with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ease and blessing. He has ordered that your charity be given to me, so give it to me.' So they gave it to him."

Then He, glorified be He, explained to them who their mothers truly are, saying: ﴿Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them﴾. That is: their mothers are only the women who bore them.

﴿And God is Acquainted with what you do﴾: nothing of your deeds is hidden from Him, so He will reward you for them.

Then He, glorified be He, mentioned the ruling for one who is unable to perform the expiation, saying: ﴿So whoever does not find [a neck], then fasting two consecutive months before they touch one another﴾. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "Three [acts of atonement] are each a mudd: the expiation for an oath, the expiation for zihar, and the expiation for [breaking a] fast."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have made zihar from my wife and I had intercourse with her before I had atoned.' Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Ansari, who said: "I was a man who had been given more desire for women than anyone else. Then one night, while she was serving me, something of her was uncovered to me, and I pounced upon her. When I rose in the morning, I went out to my people and told them my account. I said: 'Come with me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and inform him of my matter.' They said: 'No, by Allah, we will not do that. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: "That [is] the severity of the expiation by which you are admonished": that is, the severity of the expiation is an admonition to you so that you abandon ẓihār.

﴿And God is Acquainted with what you do﴾: nothing of your deeds is hidden from Him, so He will reward you for them.

Then He, glorified be He, mentioned the ruling for one who is unable to perform the expiation, saying: ﴿So whoever does not find [a neck], then fasting two consecutive months before they touch one another﴾. That is: whoever does not find a neck in his possession and is not able to obtain its value, then upon him is fasting two consecutive months, successive, without breaking the fast during them. If he breaks it, he begins again if the breaking was without an excuse. If it was due to an excuse such as travel or illness, then Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabāḥ, ʿAmr ibn Dinar, al-Shaʿbi, al-Shafiʿi, and Malik said: he continues and does not begin again.

Abu Ḥanifa said: he begins again. This is also narrated from al-Shafiʿi. The meaning of "before they touch one another" is what was mentioned shortly before. So if he has intercourse by night or day, intentionally or by mistake, he begins again. This was said by Abu Ḥanifa and Malik.

Al-Shafiʿi said: he does not begin again if he has intercourse by night, because the night is not a time for fasting. The first view is more preferable.

﴿So whoever is not able﴾, meaning: to fast two consecutive months, ﴿then feeding sixty needy persons﴾: that is, upon him is to feed sixty needy persons, two mudd (مُدّ) for each needy person, which is half a ṣāʿ. This was said by Abu Ḥanifa and his companions.

Al-Shafiʿi and others said: one mudd for each needy person. The apparent meaning of the verse is that he feeds them until they are satisfied once, or gives them what satisfies them. He is not obligated to gather them all at once; rather he may feed some of the sixty on one day and others on another day.

The indication in His saying: ﴿That﴾ refers to the rulings mentioned earlier, and it is the subject, and its predicate is omitted, meaning: that is in effect, ﴿so that you may believe in God and His Messenger﴾. It is also permissible for the demonstrative to be in the accusative position, and the estimate would be: We have done that so that you may believe, that is, so that you may affirm that God commanded it and legislated it, or so that you may obey God and His Messenger in commands and prohibitions, stop at the limits of the Sharīʿa, not transgress them, and not return to ẓihār, which is an objectionable and false statement.

The indication in His saying: ﴿And these﴾ refers to the rulings mentioned, and it is the subject, and its predicate is "the limits of God." So do not transgress His limits which He set for you, for He has made clear to you that ẓihār is disobedience, and that its expiation mentioned here brings pardon and forgiveness. ﴿And for the disbelievers﴾, those who do not stop at the limits of God and do not act by what God has set for His servants, ﴿there is a painful punishment﴾, which is the punishment of Hell. He called it disbelief (kufr) as an intensification and severity.

Ibn Māja, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "Blessed is He whose hearing encompasses everything! Indeed I heard the speech of Khawla bint Thaʿlaba, and some of it was hidden from me, while she was complaining about her husband to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and she was saying: 'O Messenger of God, my youth has been consumed by him, and I have spread out my belly for him [bearing children]; until when my age has grown old and my children have ceased, he has performed ẓihār against me. O God, I complain to You.'" She said: "She did not leave until Gabriel descended with these verses: ﴿God has indeed heard the statement of her who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾." He was Aws ibn al-Ṣāmit.

Al-Naḥḥas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The first person to perform ẓihār in Islam was Aws. He had a paternal cousin's daughter named Khawla bint Khuwaylid, and he performed ẓihār against her. He was dismayed, and said: 'I see you have become unlawful to me.' So go to the Prophet (ﷺ) and ask him." She came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and found with him the one who combed his hair, and she informed him. He said: "O Khawla, we have not been commanded anything regarding your matter." Then God revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "O Khawla, rejoice." She said: "Good." He said: "Good." Then he recited to her: ﴿God has indeed heard the statement of her who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾ and the verses.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 58, verses 1–4 (part 2 of 2):

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related, by way of Yusuf ibn Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "Khawlah bint Tha'labah narrated to me, saying: 'By Allah, it was concerning me and Aws ibn al-Samit that Allah revealed the opening of Surat al-Mujadilah.' She said: 'I was with him, and he was an elderly man whose temper had become bad. He came in to me one day and I argued with him about something, and he became angry and said: "You are to me like the back of my mother" (anti 'alayya ka-zahri ummi). Then he went out and sat in his people's gathering for a while, then came in to me, and behold, he wanted me for himself. I said: "No, by Him in whose hand is Khawlah's soul! You shall not reach me, after what you have said, until Allah and His Messenger judge concerning us."' Then I went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him of that. I had not left before the Qur'an was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was overcome by what usually overcame him, then it was lifted from him, and he said to me: 'O Khawlah, Allah has revealed concerning you and your companion.' Then he recited to me: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of she who argues with you﴾ until His words: ﴿a painful punishment﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Tell him to free a slave.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he has no means to free a slave.' He said: 'Then let him fast two consecutive months.' I said: 'By Allah, he is an elderly man who has no capacity for fasting.' He said: 'Then let him feed sixty needy persons, a wasq of dates.' I said: 'By Allah, he does not have that.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I will assist him with an 'araq of dates.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I too will assist him with another 'araq.' He said: 'You have done right and done well. Go and give it in charity on his behalf, then treat your cousin kindly.' She said: 'So I did.'" There are other hadiths on this topic.

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi, in his Sunan, related from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿then they return to what they said﴾, that he said: "It is the man who says to his wife: 'You are to me like the back of my mother.' When he says this, it is not lawful for him to approach her, by marriage or otherwise, until he atones by freeing a slave. If he does not find one, then [he must fast] two consecutive months before they touch one another. 'Touching' means intercourse. If he is unable, then [he must feed] sixty needy persons. If he says to her, 'You are to me like the back of my mother if you do such-and-such,' then zihar (the pre-Islamic divorce formula of likening a wife to one's mother) does not take effect in that until he breaks the condition; if he breaks it, he must not approach her until he atones. Divorce does not take effect through zihar."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "Three [acts of atonement] are each a mudd: the expiation for an oath, the expiation for zihar, and the expiation for [breaking a] fast."

al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I have made zihar from my wife, and I saw the whiteness of her anklet in the light of the moon, and I had intercourse with her before I had atoned.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Did Allah not say: "before they touch one another"?' He said: 'I have done it, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Refrain from her until you atone.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have made zihar from my wife and I had intercourse with her before I had atoned.' He said: 'What led you to that?' He said: 'I saw her anklet in the light of the moon.' He said: 'Do not approach her until you do what Allah has commanded you.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Ansari, who said: "I was a man who had been given more desire for women than anyone else. When Ramadan came, I made zihar from my wife until Ramadan should end, out of fear that I might have intercourse with her during my nights, and so I would continue in that and not be able to restrain myself until morning overtook me. Then one night, while she was serving me, something of her was uncovered to me, and I pounced upon her. When I rose in the morning, I went out to my people and told them my account. I said: 'Come with me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and inform him of my matter.' They said: 'No, by Allah, we will not do that. We fear that the Qur'an may be revealed concerning us, or that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) may say about us a saying whose shame will remain upon us. But go yourself and do what seems right to you.' So I went out and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him my account. He said: 'Is it so with you?' I said: 'It is so with me.' He said: 'Is it so with you?' I said: 'It is so with me.' He said: 'Is it so with you?' I said: 'It is so with me. Here I am, so execute upon me the judgment of Allah, for I am patient in that.' He said: 'Free a slave.' I struck my neck with my hand and said: 'No, by Him who sent you with the truth, I have not come to own anything but this.' He said: 'Then fast two consecutive months.' I said: 'Has what befell me befallen me except through fasting?' He said: 'Then feed sixty needy persons.' I said: 'By Him who sent you with the truth, we spent this night of ours hungry, with no supper.' He said: 'Go to the official in charge of the charity of Banu Zurayq, and tell him to hand it over to you, and feed sixty needy persons from it with a wasq on your behalf, and then use the rest of it for yourself and your dependants.' So I returned to my people and said: 'I found among you narrowness and bad judgment, and I found with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ease and blessing. He has ordered that your charity be given to me, so give it to me.' So they gave it to him."

(p-1464) It is Madani.

Al-Qurtubi said: "This is the consensus, except for a narration from ʿAṭāʾ that the first ten verses of it are Madani and the rest Makki." Al-Kalbi said: "All of it was revealed in Madina, except His saying: ﴿There is no secret conversation among three but He is the fourth of them﴾, which was revealed in Makka."

Ibn al-Ḍurays, al-Naḥḥas, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-ʿAẓama*, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Surat al-Mujadila was revealed in Madina."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿God has indeed heard﴾. Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisaʾi read it with idgham (assimilation) of the dal into the sin, while the rest read it with izhar (clear pronunciation) of the dal.

Al-Kisaʾi said: "Whoever makes the dal clear before the sin, his tongue is non-Arabic (ʿajami) and not Arabic." ﴿The statement of her who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾, meaning she argues with you about the matter of her husband, ﴿and complains to God﴾, is coordinated (ʿaṭf) on "disputes with you."

The dispute in question was this: whenever he said to her, "You have become unlawful to me," she would say, "By God, he has not mentioned divorce." Then she would say, "I complain to God of my poverty and my loneliness, and I have young children: if I join them to him, they are lost, and if I join them to me, they go hungry." She began raising her head to the sky and saying, "O God, I complain to You." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and complains to God﴾.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: This verse was revealed about Khawla bint Thaʿlaba and her husband Aws ibn al-Samit, who had a touch of madness (lamam). One day his madness intensified, and he performed ẓihār against her (zihar, a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a man likens his wife to a woman forbidden to him, such as his mother), then he regretted it. At that time, ẓihār was a form of divorce in the Jahiliyya.

It was also said that she was Khawla bint Hakim, and it was said that her name was Jamila. The first view is more sound. It was also said that she was the daughter of Khuwaylid.

Al-Mawardi said: She was attributed sometimes to her father and sometimes to her grandfather, and both are correct: her father and her grandfather. So she is Khawla bint Thaʿlaba ibn Khuwaylid.

The clause ﴿God hears your conversation﴾ is either in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or it is a resumed clause (mustaʾnafa) functioning as a reason (taʿlil) for what precedes it. That is: God knows your mutual argument in speech.

﴿Indeed God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾: He hears everything that is heard and sees everything that is seen, and among that is what this woman argued with you about.

Then He, glorified be He, explained the matter of ẓihār itself and mentioned its ruling, saying: ﴿Those of you who perform ẓihār against their wives﴾. The majority read yuẓahharūn (يَظَّهَّرُونَ) with shadda and a fatḥa on the first letter of the imperfect. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi read yuẓāhirūn (يُظّاهِرُونَ) with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, shadda on the ẓāʾ, and an added alif. Abu al-ʿAliya, ʿAsim, and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh read yuẓāhirūn (يُظاهِرُونَ) with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, a light pronunciation of the ẓāʾ, and a kasra on the hāʾ.

Something similar to this has already been discussed in Surat al-Aḥzab.

Ubayy read yataẓāharūn (يَتَظاهَرُونَ), with the assimilation undone.

The meaning of ẓihār is that a man says to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother." There is no disagreement that this is ẓihār.

They differed if he says, "You are to me like the back of my daughter," or "my sister," or anything else of those women who are unlawful to him by kinship. A group, including Abu Ḥanifa and Malik, held that this is ẓihār, and this was the view of al-Ḥasan, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Zuhri, al-Awzaʿi, and al-Thawri.

A group including Qatada and al-Shaʿbi said that it is not ẓihār, but that ẓihār is specific to the mother alone.

The narrations from al-Shafiʿi differed: it was narrated from him in the manner of the first view, and it was narrated from him in the manner of the second view. The root of ẓihār is derived from ẓahr (back).

They differed if he says to his wife, "You are to me like the head of my mother, or her hand, or her leg, or something similar." Is it ẓihār or not? The same applies if he says, "You are to me like my mother," without mentioning the back. The apparent view is that if he intends ẓihār by that, it is ẓihār.

It was narrated from Abu Ḥanifa that if he likens her to a part of his mother's body which it is permissible for him to look at, it is not ẓihār.

It was narrated from al-Shafiʿi that ẓihār occurs only when it is by the back alone.

They differed if he likens his wife to a foreign woman. It was said that it is ẓihār, and it was said that it is not. The discussion of this is extensive in the books of furūʿ (positive law).

The clause ﴿they are not their mothers﴾ is in the nominative position (maḥall rafʿ), as the predicate of the relative clause. That is: their wives are not their mothers. So that is a lie on their part, and in this there is rebuke and reproach for those who perform ẓihār.

The majority read ʾummahātihim (أُمَّهاتِهِمْ) in the accusative, according to the Ḥijazi dialect in which mā functions like laysa (in governing the predicate). Abu ʿAmr and al-Sulami read it in the nominative, without this governing, and this is the dialect of Najd and Banu Asad.

Then He, glorified be He, explained to them who their mothers truly are, saying: ﴿Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them﴾. That is: their mothers are only the women who bore them.

Then He increased in rebuke and censure of them, saying: ﴿And indeed they utter an objectionable word and a lie﴾. That is: those who perform ẓihār indeed utter with this statement an objectionable word, that is, a repugnant word that the Sharīʿa rejects. Zūr (زُورًا) means falsehood. Munkaran and zūran are in the accusative because they are adjectives of a verbal noun that has been omitted, meaning: a statement that is objectionable and false.

﴿And indeed God is Most Pardoning, Most Forgiving﴾: that is, abundant in pardon and forgiveness, since He made the expiation (kaffāra) upon them a means of freeing them from this objectionable statement.

﴿And those who perform ẓihār against their wives, then go back on what they said﴾. When He, glorified be He, mentioned ẓihār in general and rebuked those who commit it, He began detailing its rulings. The meaning is: those who say that objectionable and false statement, then go back on what they said, that is, return to what they said by making amends and retracting it, as in His saying: ﴿that you should never return to the like of it﴾ (Qur'an 24:17), that is, to its like.

Al-Akhfash said: "li-mā qālū" (لِما قالُوا) and "ilā mā qālū" (إلى ما قالُوا) are interchangeable. He cited: ﴿And they said, "Praise belongs to God, who guided us to this"﴾ (7:43); and He said: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ (37:23); and He said: ﴿because your Lord has inspired her﴾ (99:5); and He said: ﴿And it was revealed to Noah﴾ (11:36).

Al-Farrāʾ said: the lām (ل) has the sense of "ʿan" (عَنْ, "from"), and the meaning is: then they retract what they said and intend intercourse.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: then they return to the intention of sexual intercourse on account of what they said.

Al-Akhfash also said: the verse has inversion (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr). The meaning is: those who perform ẓihār against their wives, then go back to what they were doing of intercourse, ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾ for what they said, that is: upon them is the freeing of a neck on account of what they said.

So the preposition in His saying "li-mā qālū" is connected to the omitted element which is the predicate of the subject, which is "upon them" (fa-ʿalayhim).

The people of knowledge differed in interpreting the mentioned "return" (ʿawd) in several views:

The first: it is the determination to have intercourse. This was said by the Iraqis, Abu Ḥanifa and his companions. It was also narrated from Malik.

It was said: it is the intercourse itself. This was said by al-Ḥasan, and it was also narrated from Malik.

It was said: it is that he keeps her as a wife after ẓihār while having the ability to divorce. This was said by al-Shafiʿi.

It was said: it is the expiation, and the meaning is that he may not have intercourse with her except by means of expiation. This was said by al-Layth ibn Saʿd, and it was narrated from Abu Ḥanifa.

It was said: it is repeating the ẓihār by its wording. This was said by the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Ẓāhir). It was narrated from Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj, Abu al-ʿAliya, and al-Farrāʾ. The meaning is: then they return to the statement of what they said.

The relative clause is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾, on the assumption of "upon them the freeing of a neck," as mentioned earlier. Or: then what is obligatory upon them is the manumission of a neck. One says ḥarrartuhu (حَرَّرْتُهُ), meaning: I made him free. The apparent view is that any neck suffices. It was said that it must be a believing neck, like the neck in the expiation for murder. The first view was held by Abu Ḥanifa and his companions, and the second by Malik and al-Shafiʿi, who also required that it be free of every defect.

﴿Before they touch one another﴾: the touching here means intercourse. This was said by the majority. So it is not permissible for the one who performed ẓihār to have intercourse until he makes expiation. It was said that the intended meaning is enjoyment through intercourse, touching, or looking at the private part with desire. This was said by Malik, and it is one of the two views of al-Shafiʿi.

The indication in His saying: ﴿That﴾ refers to the ruling mentioned, and it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿you are admonished with it﴾, that is, you are commanded with it, or you are restrained from committing ẓihār by it. In this is a clarification of what the purpose of prescribing expiation is.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: "That [is] the severity of the expiation by which you are admonished": that is, the severity of the expiation is an admonition to you so that you abandon ẓihār.

﴿And God is Acquainted with what you do﴾: nothing of your deeds is hidden from Him, so He will reward you for them.

Then He, glorified be He, mentioned the ruling for one who is unable to perform the expiation, saying: ﴿So whoever does not find [a neck], then fasting two consecutive months before they touch one another﴾. That is: whoever does not find a neck in his possession and is not able to obtain its value, then upon him is fasting two consecutive months, successive, without breaking the fast during them. If he breaks it, he begins again if the breaking was without an excuse. If it was due to an excuse such as travel or illness, then Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabāḥ, ʿAmr ibn Dinar, al-Shaʿbi, al-Shafiʿi, and Malik said: he continues and does not begin again.

Abu Ḥanifa said: he begins again. This is also narrated from al-Shafiʿi. The meaning of "before they touch one another" is what was mentioned shortly before. So if he has intercourse by night or day, intentionally or by mistake, he begins again. This was said by Abu Ḥanifa and Malik.

Al-Shafiʿi said: he does not begin again if he has intercourse by night, because the night is not a time for fasting. The first view is more preferable.

﴿So whoever is not able﴾, meaning: to fast two consecutive months, ﴿then feeding sixty needy persons﴾: that is, upon him is to feed sixty needy persons, two mudd (مُدّ) for each needy person, which is half a ṣāʿ. This was said by Abu Ḥanifa and his companions.

Al-Shafiʿi and others said: one mudd for each needy person. The apparent meaning of the verse is that he feeds them until they are satisfied once, or gives them what satisfies them. He is not obligated to gather them all at once; rather he may feed some of the sixty on one day and others on another day.

The indication in His saying: ﴿That﴾ refers to the rulings mentioned earlier, and it is the subject, and its predicate is omitted, meaning: that is in effect, ﴿so that you may believe in God and His Messenger﴾. It is also permissible for the demonstrative to be in the accusative position, and the estimate would be: We have done that so that you may believe, that is, so that you may affirm that God commanded it and legislated it, or so that you may obey God and His Messenger in commands and prohibitions, stop at the limits of the Sharīʿa, not transgress them, and not return to ẓihār, which is an objectionable and false statement.

The indication in His saying: ﴿And these﴾ refers to the rulings mentioned, and it is the subject, and its predicate is "the limits of God." So do not transgress His limits which He set for you, for He has made clear to you that ẓihār is disobedience, and that its expiation mentioned here brings pardon and forgiveness. ﴿And for the disbelievers﴾, those who do not stop at the limits of God and do not act by what God has set for His servants, ﴿there is a painful punishment﴾, which is the punishment of Hell. He called it disbelief (kufr) as an intensification and severity.

Ibn Māja, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "Blessed is He whose hearing encompasses everything! Indeed I heard the speech of Khawla bint Thaʿlaba, and some of it was hidden from me, while she was complaining about her husband to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and she was saying: 'O Messenger of God, my youth has been consumed by him, and I have spread out my belly for him [bearing children]; until when my age has grown old and my children have ceased, he has performed ẓihār against me. O God, I complain to You.'" She said: "She did not leave until Gabriel descended with these verses: ﴿God has indeed heard the statement of her who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾." He was Aws ibn al-Ṣāmit.

Al-Naḥḥas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The first person to perform ẓihār in Islam was Aws. He had a paternal cousin's daughter named Khawla bint Khuwaylid, and he performed ẓihār against her. He was dismayed, and said: 'I see you have become unlawful to me.' So go to the Prophet (ﷺ) and ask him." She came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and found with him the one who combed his hair, and she informed him. He said: "O Khawla, we have not been commanded anything regarding your matter." Then God revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "O Khawla, rejoice." She said: "Good." He said: "Good." Then he recited to her: ﴿God has indeed heard the statement of her who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾ and the verses.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 58, verses 1–4 (part 2 of 2):

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related, by way of Yusuf ibn Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "Khawlah bint Tha'labah narrated to me, saying: 'By Allah, it was concerning me and Aws ibn al-Samit that Allah revealed the opening of Surat al-Mujadilah.' She said: 'I was with him, and he was an elderly man whose temper had become bad. He came in to me one day and I argued with him about something, and he became angry and said: "You are to me like the back of my mother" (anti 'alayya ka-zahri ummi). Then he went out and sat in his people's gathering for a while, then came in to me, and behold, he wanted me for himself. I said: "No, by Him in whose hand is Khawlah's soul! You shall not reach me, after what you have said, until Allah and His Messenger judge concerning us."' Then I went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him of that. I had not left before the Qur'an was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was overcome by what usually overcame him, then it was lifted from him, and he said to me: 'O Khawlah, Allah has revealed concerning you and your companion.' Then he recited to me: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of she who argues with you﴾ until His words: ﴿a painful punishment﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Tell him to free a slave.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he has no means to free a slave.' He said: 'Then let him fast two consecutive months.' I said: 'By Allah, he is an elderly man who has no capacity for fasting.' He said: 'Then let him feed sixty needy persons, a wasq of dates.' I said: 'By Allah, he does not have that.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I will assist him with an 'araq of dates.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I too will assist him with another 'araq.' He said: 'You have done right and done well. Go and give it in charity on his behalf, then treat your cousin kindly.' She said: 'So I did.'" There are other hadiths on this topic.

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi, in his Sunan, related from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿then they return to what they said﴾, that he said: "It is the man who says to his wife: 'You are to me like the back of my mother.' When he says this, it is not lawful for him to approach her, by marriage or otherwise, until he atones by freeing a slave. If he does not find one, then [he must fast] two consecutive months before they touch one another. 'Touching' means intercourse. If he is unable, then [he must feed] sixty needy persons. If he says to her, 'You are to me like the back of my mother if you do such-and-such,' then zihar (the pre-Islamic divorce formula of likening a wife to one's mother) does not take effect in that until he breaks the condition; if he breaks it, he must not approach her until he atones. Divorce does not take effect through zihar."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "Three [acts of atonement] are each a mudd: the expiation for an oath, the expiation for zihar, and the expiation for [breaking a] fast."

al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I have made zihar from my wife, and I saw the whiteness of her anklet in the light of the moon, and I had intercourse with her before I had atoned.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Did Allah not say: "before they touch one another"?' He said: 'I have done it, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Refrain from her until you atone.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have made zihar from my wife and I had intercourse with her before I had atoned.' He said: 'What led you to that?' He said: 'I saw her anklet in the light of the moon.' He said: 'Do not approach her until you do what Allah has commanded you.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Ansari, who said: "I was a man who had been given more desire for women than anyone else. When Ramadan came, I made zihar from my wife until Ramadan should end, out of fear that I might have intercourse with her during my nights, and so I would continue in that and not be able to restrain myself until morning overtook me. Then one night, while she was serving me, something of her was uncovered to me, and I pounced upon her. When I rose in the morning, I went out to my people and told them my account. I said: 'Come with me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and inform him of my matter.' They said: 'No, by Allah, we will not do that. We fear that the Qur'an may be revealed concerning us, or that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) may say about us a saying whose shame will remain upon us. But go yourself and do what seems right to you.' So I went out and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him my account. He said: 'Is it so with you?' I said: 'It is so with me.' He said: 'Is it so with you?' I said: 'It is so with me.' He said: 'Is it so with you?' I said: 'It is so with me. Here I am, so execute upon me the judgment of Allah, for I am patient in that.' He said: 'Free a slave.' I struck my neck with my hand and said: 'No, by Him who sent you with the truth, I have not come to own anything but this.' He said: 'Then fast two consecutive months.' I said: 'Has what befell me befallen me except through fasting?' He said: 'Then feed sixty needy persons.' I said: 'By Him who sent you with the truth, we spent this night of ours hungry, with no supper.' He said: 'Go to the official in charge of the charity of Banu Zurayq, and tell him to hand it over to you, and feed sixty needy persons from it with a wasq on your behalf, and then use the rest of it for yourself and your dependants.' So I returned to my people and said: 'I found among you narrowness and bad judgment, and I found with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ease and blessing. He has ordered that your charity be given to me, so give it to me.' So they gave it to him."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 58, verses 5–10 (part 1 of 2):

His saying ﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾. When Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the believers who stand at His limits (ḥudūd), He mentioned those who oppose (al-muḥāddīn). Al-muḥāddah (opposition) means hostility (al-mushāqqah), enmity (al-mu'ādāh) and contradiction (al-mukhālafah). Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-muḥāddah is that one is on a limit (ḥadd) that opposes one's companion, and its origin is resistance (al-mumāna'ah), and from it comes al-ḥadīd (iron), and from it al-haddād (the blacksmith) for the gatekeeper (al-bawwāb).

﴿They will be humiliated (kubitū) as those before them were humiliated (kubita)﴾, i.e., they will be disgraced and abased. It is said: Allah kabata so-and-so when He abased him, and one who is repelled with humiliation is called maktūb.

Al-Muqatilān said: they will be disgraced as those before them from among the people of polytheism were disgraced. Qatādah said likewise.

Abū 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: they will be destroyed (uhlikū).

Ibn Zayd said: they will be punished (ʿudhdhibū).

Al-Suddī said: they will be cursed (lu'inū).

Al-Farrā' said: they will be enraged (ughīẓū).

The intended meaning of ﴿those before them﴾ is the unbelievers of the past nations who were hostile to the messengers of Allah. He expressed the future with the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence. It was also said that the meaning is in the past tense, and that refers to what befell the polytheists on the day of Badr, for Allah humbled them through killing, capture and subjugation.

The clause ﴿and We have certainly sent down clear signs﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the waw in kubitū: that is, while in fact We have sent down clear signs concerning those among the earlier nations who opposed Allah and His messengers. It was said that what is meant is the obligations (farā'iḍ) which Allah, glory be to Him, sent down; and it was said they are the miracles (mu'jizāt). ﴿And for the unbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾, i.e., for the unbelievers in everything that must be believed in, so the signs mentioned here enter first and foremost. The humiliating punishment is that which humiliates its owner, abases him, and takes away his honour.

﴿On the day Allah will resurrect them all﴾. The time expression (al-ẓarf) is in the accusative, governed either by an implied "remember" (udhkur), or by "humiliating" (muhīn), or by what the preposition (lām) is attached to of settledness (al-istiqrār), or by "has enumerated it" (aḥṣāhu) mentioned after it. The accusative of "all" (jamīʿan) is as a circumstantial state: that is, gathered together in one state; or He resurrects them all, none of them left unresurrected, and then He informs them of what they did, i.e., informs them of the ugly deeds they did in the world, as a rebuke and reproach to them and to complete the proof against them. The clause ﴿Allah has enumerated it, and they have forgotten it﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafah), an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: how will He inform them of that, given its abundance and the variety of its kinds? So it was said: Allah has enumerated it all, and nothing of it has escaped Him.

The state is that they have forgotten it and did not preserve it; rather they found it present and written in their records. ﴿And Allah is Witness over everything﴾: nothing of things is hidden from Him; rather He is aware and observant.

Then, glory be to Him, emphasised the demonstration of His being knowing of everything, and said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth?﴾, i.e., do you not know that His knowledge encompasses what is in them, such that nothing of what is in them is hidden from Him? The clause "There is not a private conversation of three" etc. is a resumptive clause, establishing the comprehensiveness and encompassing of His knowledge of all knowable things.

Al-Jumhūr read yakūnu with the letter yā' (third person). Abū Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qā', al-A'raj and Abū Ḥaywah read it with the letter tā' (second person). Kāna in both readings is complete (tāmmah), min is extra for emphasis, and najwā is the subject of kāna. Al-najwā is secret conversation; it is said: qawmun najwā, i.e., one who has a secret conversation, and it is a verbal noun.

The meaning is: there is not found any secret conversation of three or of those who converse privately. It is permissible for najwā to be applied to the persons conversing secretly. On the first reading, thalāthah is in the genitive by being an annexed noun to najwā; and on the other two readings its genitive is by apposition (badal) from najwā or as its attribute.

Al-Farrā' said: "thalāthatun" is an attribute of najwā, so it is in the genitive; if you wish, you may annex najwā to it. If you put it in the accusative by implying a verb, it is permissible, and this is the reading of Ibn Abī 'Ablah. It is also permissible to put thalāthatun in the nominative as an apposition from the position of najwā.

﴿Except that He is their fourth﴾: this clause is in an accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and likewise His saying "except that He is their sixth" and "except that He is with them". The meaning is: no such thing exists except in a state of one of these states, so the exception is an exception from the most general of states. The meaning of "their fourth" is making them four; likewise "their sixth" is making them six, in that He shares with them in knowledge of that secret conversation. ﴿Nor fewer than that, nor more﴾: i.e., nor a secret conversation of five; the specification of the two numbers in mention is because the most common practice of those conversing privately is to be three or five, or the event which was the occasion of revelation involved people who were three in one place and five in another.

Al-Farrā' said: the number is not intended, for He, glory be to Him, is with every number, few or many, knowing the secret and the open; nothing of it is hidden from Him. ﴿Nor less than that, nor more, but He is with them﴾: i.e., nor fewer than the number mentioned, such as one or two, nor more than it, such as six or seven, except that He is with them, knowing what they confide, nothing of it hidden from Him.

Al-Jumhūr read "wa-lā akthara" in the genitive with a fatḥah, as a conjunction to the wording of najwā. Al-Ḥasan, al-A'mash, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Abū Ḥaywah, Ya'qūb, Abū al-'Āliyah, Naṣr, 'Īsā ibn 'Umar and Salām read it in the nominative as a conjunction to the position (maḥall) of najwā. Al-Jumhūr read "wa-lā akthara" with the letter thā' (three dots), while al-Zuhrī and 'Ikrimah read it with the letter bā' (one dot).

Al-Wāḥidī said: the exegetes said: the hypocrites and the Jews used to converse secretly among themselves and give the believers to understand that they were conversing about what would grieve them, so they were saddened by that. When this went on for a long time and became frequent, they complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he commanded them not to converse secretly apart from the Muslims. They did not desist from that and returned to their private conversations, so Allah revealed these verses. The meaning of "wherever they are" is the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of every secret conversation that occurs among them in whatever place. ﴿Then He will inform them﴾, i.e., He will inform them on the Day of Resurrection of what they did, as a rebuke and reproach to them and a binding of the proof. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of everything﴾: nothing is hidden from Him, whatever it may be.

﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret conversation, then they return to what they were forbidden?﴾ Those who were forbidden and then returned to what they were forbidden are those previously mentioned, from among the hypocrites and the Jews.

Muqatil said: there was an agreement between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Jews, so when a man from among the believers passed by them, they conversed among themselves until the believer would think evil, so Allah forbade them, but they did not desist, and so it was revealed.

Ibn Zayd said: a man would come to the Prophet (ﷺ), ask him for a need and converse with him, and the land on that day was at war, so they would imagine that he was conversing with him about war, or a calamity, or an important matter, so they would be alarmed by that, and they would converse secretly about sin, transgression and disobedience to the Messenger.

Al-Jumhūr read "yatanājawna" in the pattern yatafā'alūna. Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim chose this reading because of His later saying: "When you converse secretly, do not converse secretly..." Ḥamzah, Khalaf and Warsh on the authority of Ya'qūb read "yantajūna" in the pattern yaftaʿilūna, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ūd and his companions. Sībawayh related that tafā'ala and ifta'ala come with one meaning, like takhāṣamū and ikhtaṣamū, and taqātalū and iqtatalū.

The meaning of "sin" (ith'm) is what is sinful in itself, such as lying and injustice; "transgression" (ʿudwān) is what contains transgression against the believers; and "disobedience to the Messenger" is opposing him.

Al-Jumhūr read "wa-maʿṣiyati" in the singular. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ḥumayd and Mujāhid read "wa-maʿṣiyāti" in the plural.

﴿And when they come to you, they greet you with that by which Allah did not greet you﴾. Al-Qurṭubī said: what is meant by them are the Jews, who used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and say "as-sāmu ʿalayka" (death be upon you), meaning by it the greeting outwardly, while they intend death inwardly. So the Prophet (ﷺ) would say: "ʿAlaykum." In another narration: "wa-ʿalaykum."

﴿And they say to themselves﴾, i.e., among themselves: ﴿Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?﴾, i.e., why does He not punish us for that? If Muhammad were a prophet, He would punish us for what our saying includes of mockery of him. It was also said the meaning is: if he were a prophet, he would be answered concerning us when he says "wa-ʿalaykum", and death would have befallen us at that. ﴿Hell is sufficient for them﴾ as a punishment; ﴿they will burn in it﴾, i.e., they will enter it; ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾, i.e., the place of return, which is Hell.

﴿O you who have believed, when you converse secretly, do not converse secretly in sin and transgression and disobedience to the Messenger﴾. When Allah, glory be to Him, finished forbidding the Jews and the hypocrites from secret conversation, He guided the believers, when they converse among themselves, that they should not converse about what contains sin, transgression and disobedience to the Messenger of Allah, as the Jews and the hypocrites do.

Then He explained to them what they should converse about in their gatherings and private meetings, so He said: ﴿And converse secretly in righteousness and piety﴾, i.e., in obedience and abstaining from disobedience. It was said the address is to the hypocrites, and the meaning: O you who have believed outwardly or in their claim. Al-Zajjāj chose this. It was also said the address is to the Jews, and the meaning: O you who have believed in Moses. The first is preferable. Then Allah, glory be to Him, warned them, saying: ﴿And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered﴾, so that He will recompense you for your deeds.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained that what the Jews and hypocrites do of secret conversation comes from Satan, so He said: ﴿Secret conversation is only from Satan﴾, meaning with sin, transgression and disobedience to the Messenger, ﴿from Satan﴾ and not from anyone else, i.e., from his adornment and enticement. ﴿That he may grieve those who have believed﴾, i.e., in order to bring them into grief through what occurs to them of the imagining that they are in a plot against them. ﴿But it will not harm them at all﴾, or: neither Satan nor the secret conversation which Satan adorns will harm the believers in any harm, except by the permission of Allah, i.e., by His will. It was also said: by His knowledge. ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾, i.e., let them entrust their affairs to Him, commit themselves to Him in all their affairs, seek refuge in Allah from Satan, and not be concerned about what he adorns of secret conversation.

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Bazzār, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab have transmitted — al-Suyūṭī said with a good chain — from Ibn ʿUmar: The Jews used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "as-sāmu ʿalayka," intending by it to revile him; then they would say to themselves: "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?" So this verse was revealed: ﴿And when they come to you, they greet you with that by which Allah did not greet you﴾.

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Bukhārī, and al-Tirmidhī, who authenticated it, transmitted from Anas: "A Jew came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions and said: 'as-sāmu ʿalaykum.' The people replied to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do you know what this one said?' They said: 'Allah knows best, O Prophet of Allah, he greeted (salām).' He said: 'No, but he said such and such. Return it to me.' So they returned it to him. He said: 'Did you say: as-sāmu ʿalaykum?' He said: 'Yes.' The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: 'When one of the People of the Book greets you, say: ʿalayka.' He said: 'ʿAlayka what you said.'"

He said: ﴿And when they come to you, they greet you with that by which Allah did not greet you﴾.

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others transmitted from ʿĀ'ishah, she said: "Some Jews entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'as-sāmu ʿalayka, O Abū al-Qāsim.' ʿĀ'ishah said: 'Upon you be the poison and the curse.' He said: 'O ʿĀ'ishah, Allah does not love obscenity or the one who is obscene.' I said: 'Do you not hear what they say, as-sām?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Did you not hear me say: wa-ʿalaykum?' So Allah revealed: ﴿And when they come to you, they greet you with that by which Allah did not greet you﴾."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning this verse, he said: "The hypocrites used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when they greeted him: 'Sām ʿalayka,' so it was revealed."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, he said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) sent out a detachment (sariyyah) and dispatched it to fight, the hypocrites would meet the Muslims, nodding their heads towards them and saying: 'The people have been killed.' And when they saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they would converse secretly and show sorrow. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, when you converse secretly, do not converse secretly in sin and transgression and disobedience to the Messenger﴾ — the verse."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When there are three of you, two should not confide together apart from the third, for that would grieve him."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: "We would take turns attending the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at his door. If he commanded or forbade something, those on duty would increase in number, and the volunteers would gather at night. When we were gathered, talking, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us at night and said: 'What is this private conversation? Were you not forbidden from private conversation?' We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we were mentioning the Messiah, out of fear of him.' He said: 'Shall I not inform you of what I fear for you more than that?' We said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'The hidden shirk: that a man stands up and performs an action so that others may see him.'"

Ibn Kathir said: This is a gharib (weak-isnad, singular-transmission) chain, and in it there is some weakness (da'if) among the narrators.

﴿They will be humiliated (kubitū) as those before them were humiliated (kubita)﴾, i.e., they will be disgraced and abased. It is said: Allah kabata so-and-so when He abased him, and one who is repelled with humiliation is called maktūb.

Al-Muqatilān said: they will be disgraced as those before them from among the people of polytheism were disgraced. Qatādah said likewise.

Abū 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: they will be destroyed (uhlikū).

Ibn Zayd said: they will be punished (ʿudhdhibū).

Al-Suddī said: they will be cursed (lu'inū).

Al-Farrā' said: they will be enraged (ughīẓū).

The intended meaning of ﴿those before them﴾ is the unbelievers of the past nations who were hostile to the messengers of Allah. He expressed the future with the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence. It was also said that the meaning is in the past tense, and that refers to what befell the polytheists on the day of Badr, for Allah humbled them through killing, capture and subjugation.

The clause ﴿and We have certainly sent down clear signs﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the waw in kubitū: that is, while in fact We have sent down clear signs concerning those among the earlier nations who opposed Allah and His messengers. It was said that what is meant is the obligations (farā'iḍ) which Allah, glory be to Him, sent down; and it was said they are the miracles (mu'jizāt). ﴿And for the unbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾, i.e., for the unbelievers in everything that must be believed in, so the signs mentioned here enter first and foremost. The humiliating punishment is that which humiliates its owner, abases him, and takes away his honour.

﴿On the day Allah will resurrect them all﴾. The time expression (al-ẓarf) is in the accusative, governed either by an implied "remember" (udhkur), or by "humiliating" (muhīn), or by what the preposition (lām) is attached to of settledness (al-istiqrār), or by "has enumerated it" (aḥṣāhu) mentioned after it. The accusative of "all" (jamīʿan) is as a circumstantial state: that is, gathered together in one state; or He resurrects them all, none of them left unresurrected, and then He informs them of what they did, i.e., informs them of the ugly deeds they did in the world, as a rebuke and reproach to them and to complete the proof against them. The clause ﴿Allah has enumerated it, and they have forgotten it﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafah), an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: how will He inform them of that, given its abundance and the variety of its kinds? So it was said: Allah has enumerated it all, and nothing of it has escaped Him.

The state is that they have forgotten it and did not preserve it; rather they found it present and written in their records. ﴿And Allah is Witness over everything﴾: nothing of things is hidden from Him; rather He is aware and observant.

Then, glory be to Him, emphasised the demonstration of His being knowing of everything, and said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth?﴾, i.e., do you not know that His knowledge encompasses what is in them, such that nothing of what is in them is hidden from Him? The clause "There is not a private conversation of three" etc. is a resumptive clause, establishing the comprehensiveness and encompassing of His knowledge of all knowable things.

Al-Jumhūr read yakūnu with the letter yā' (third person). Abū Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qā', al-A'raj and Abū Ḥaywah read it with the letter tā' (second person). Kāna in both readings is complete (tāmmah), min is extra for emphasis, and najwā is the subject of kāna. Al-najwā is secret conversation; it is said: qawmun najwā, i.e., one who has a secret conversation, and it is a verbal noun.

The meaning is: there is not found any secret conversation of three or of those who converse privately. It is permissible for najwā to be applied to the persons conversing secretly. On the first reading, thalāthah is in the genitive by being an annexed noun to najwā; and on the other two readings its genitive is by apposition (badal) from najwā or as its attribute.

Al-Farrā' said: "thalāthatun" is an attribute of najwā, so it is in the genitive; if you wish, you may annex najwā to it. If you put it in the accusative by implying a verb, it is permissible, and this is the reading of Ibn Abī 'Ablah. It is also permissible to put thalāthatun in the nominative as an apposition from the position of najwā.

The meaning is: no such thing exists except in a state of one of these states, so the exception is an exception from the most general of states. The meaning of "their fourth" is making them four; likewise "their sixth" is making them six, in that He shares with them in knowledge of that secret conversation. ﴿Nor fewer than that, nor more﴾: i.e., nor a secret conversation of five; the specification of the two numbers in mention is because the most common practice of those conversing privately is to be three or five, or the event which was the occasion of revelation involved people who were three in one place and five in another.

Al-Farrā' said: the number is not intended, for He, glory be to Him, is with every number, few or many, knowing the secret and the open; nothing of it is hidden from Him. ﴿Nor less than that, nor more, but He is with them﴾: i.e., nor fewer than the number mentioned, such as one or two, nor more than it, such as six or seven, except that He is with them, knowing what they confide, nothing of it hidden from Him.

Al-Jumhūr read "wa-lā akthara" in the genitive with a fatḥah, as a conjunction to the wording of najwā.
